title: Coding copilots: Completion speed excludes checking costs
desc: Finds a narrow randomized time benefit while distinguishing acceptance, verification, interaction and developer experience.

kps.k: AI coding assistance can accelerate task completion while creating substantial human checking and interaction work; these findings measure different aspects of productivity.
kps.d: The cluster distinguishes faster delivery from the work required to obtain, understand and verify generated code. Grounded Copilot identifies acceleration—executing an existing plan—and exploration—using suggestions to discover an approach. CUPS measures the activities surrounding suggestions. Neither interaction study estimates a comparative productivity effect, so their observations of overhead do not contradict the randomized trial’s completion-time gains.

qs.q: In acceleration mode, a programmer uses Copilot to execute their planned code actions, by completing a logical unit of code or a comment.
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

qs.q: We do not include a baseline condition where participants perform the coding task without Copilot, as this work focuses on understanding and modeling the interaction with the current version of Copilot.
qs.a: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming (CUPS study) · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The randomized Copilot trial finds a large but narrowly defined completion-time benefit.
kps.d: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity randomly assigned 95 Upwork programmers in May–June 2022. Among task completers, treatment participants averaged 71.17 minutes versus 160.89 minutes for controls: a 55.8% reduction, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 21%–89%. The outcome was time to the first commit passing 12 tests, not long-term maintainability or comprehensive code quality. The seven-percentage-point success-rate advantage was not statistically significant. Five assigned treatment participants started without Copilot, and the authors scope their conclusion to the experimental population.

qs.q: The 95 developers were randomly assigned into control and treated groups, with 45 in the treated group and 50 in control.
qs.a: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

qs.q: Conditioning on completing the task, the average completion time from the treated  group is 71.17 minutes and 160.89 minutes for the control group.
qs.a: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

kps.k: Acceptance is not completed verification, and interaction time is not necessarily wasted time.
kps.d: CUPS finds that verifying, deferring thought, waiting, prompting and editing together occupied an average 51.5% of session time; this is neither verification time alone nor a measured net productivity loss. Participants accepted 34.0% of suggestions, but sometimes checked them only after acceptance. The authors therefore recommend measuring post-acceptance verification and subsequent code retention rather than treating acceptance as settled use. Meanwhile, 14 of 21 participants reported better flow and less searching, while six expressed code-quality concerns; these perceptions do not establish productivity or defect rates.

qs.q: More generally, the states that are specific to interaction with Copilot include: ‘Verifying Suggestions’, ‘Deferring Thought for Later’, ‘Waiting for Suggestion’, ‘Prompt Crafting’, and ‘Editing Suggestion’.
qs.a: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming (CUPS study) · Academia · 2024

qs.q: We found that the total time participants spend in these states is 51.5 % (sN = 19.3) of the average session duration.
qs.a: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming (CUPS study) · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Experience may shape both benefits and checking difficulties, but the evidence does not establish a single novice–expert pattern.
kps.d: The productivity trial reports larger gains for less experienced developers, heavier daily coders and those aged 25–44; the experience association has p = 0.0629 and does not meet a conventional 5% significance threshold. CUPS observes lower acceptance among more experienced programmers but higher acceptance among prior Copilot users, without establishing causality. Grounded Copilot documents debugging difficulties, including a participant who failed after pursuing the wrong explanation for generated code’s file-access error. It also reports less general comprehension difficulty than Vaithilingam et al.; its tentative experience-based explanation remains untested and includes an inconsistent undergraduate count. Claims that assistance expands career access remain prospective.

qs.q: We notice the acceptance rate for those with substantial programming experience is 30.0% ± 14.5 while for those without is 37.6% ± 14.6.
qs.a: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming (CUPS study) · Academia · 2024

qs.q: P9 was not able to understand and localize the error, instead spending a long time trying to add more code to perform an unrelated file flush operation.
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

kps.k: The practical design agenda combines less intrusive generation with support for continuous checking.
kps.d: CUPS reports that users accepted only 10.7% of suggestions displayed during prompt crafting. The authors interpret these suggestions as interruptions and hypothesize that programmers prefer to express prompts themselves; that explanation is not an experimentally established mechanism. Grounded Copilot recommends allowing users to fill code gaps when ready rather than imposing large blocks, and proposes always-on checking through features such as automated property-based tests and live runtime values. These proposals aim to preserve flow and reduce checking effort, but the studies do not test their effectiveness.

qs.q: Among 234 suggestions that were shown while participants were actively prompt crafting, defined as a suggestion where a programmer was prompt crafting while the suggestion was being displayed, only 10.7% were accepted.
qs.a: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming (CUPS study) · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Based on our observations, future tools should mind how large code blocks can break the user’s natural development flow, instead offering code holes for users to fill in when ready.
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

kps.k: Short studies, early tools and incomplete outcome evidence limit broader conclusions.
kps.d: CUPS studied 21 participants within one organization, mostly using Python, in sessions averaging 12.23 minutes with Copilot as of August 2022. Its self-labeling method risks inconsistent categories and excludes uncertain segments representing 6.5% of session time. Grounded Copilot studied 20 participants, mostly from academia, and acknowledges limited observation of adaptation and sensitivity to tasks, languages and changing technology. The supplied When Help Hurts fragment describes cohorts and tool familiarity but lacks interpretable outcome headings; it cannot establish fatigue or harmful verification effects. Together, these materials support claims about particular assisted-programming settings, not autonomous systems or measured effects in legal work.

qs.q: On average, participants took 12.23 minutes (sample standard deviation, sN = 3.98 minutes) to complete the coding task, with a maximum session length of 20.80 minutes.
qs.a: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming (CUPS study) · Academia · 2024

qs.q: We developed our theory through a user study with 20 participants (15 from academia and 5 from industry).
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition’s distinction between narrowly measured completion speed and the broader human work of interacting with and checking generated code. They materially develop it through complementary methods: Grounded Copilot supplies a qualitative account of acceleration, exploration and debugging difficulty, while CUPS quantifies Copilot-specific interaction states and shows why acceptance cannot be treated as completed verification. Both studies deliberately examine interaction rather than compare assisted with unaided productivity, so their evidence of checking and interaction burdens complements rather than rebuts the randomized completion-time result. Material variation lies mainly in method and evidential completeness: Grounded Copilot emphasizes user behaviour and design proposals such as continuous validation; CUPS provides telemetry-based measures and recommends post-acceptance verification and code-retention metrics; the supplied When Help Hurts fragment is too incomplete to determine effects on verification load or fatigue. These sources support conclusions about particular, short assisted-programming settings, not general claims about all researchers, autonomous systems or legal work.

qs.q: Further, instead of skewing quantitative answers to predefined research questions, we chose the grounded theory approach, with the general goal of finding patters in programmers’ behavior when they interact with Copilot; we believe this approach is complementary to the quantitative studies.
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

vlens.an: The legal-tech-vendor source supports the proposition’s narrow empirical core: in a randomized trial, Copilot substantially reduced completion time among programmers who completed the task. Its support is carefully bounded because the outcome was elapsed time to the first commit passing a 12-test suite, rather than a comprehensive measure incorporating verification effort, maintainability, defects or longer-term productivity. The source therefore does not establish the cluster’s separate claims about checking and interaction costs, but neither does it conflict with them. Material qualifications include conditioning the main estimate on task completion, a non-significant difference in success rates, five treatment participants starting without Copilot, and a specific experimental population. The source also reports heterogeneous gains, including larger estimated benefits for less-experienced developers, although the experience association falls short of the conventional 5% significance threshold; its suggestion that copilots could expand access to software careers remains prospective.

elens.an: The source accepts the proposition’s distinction between completion speed and the broader work surrounding AI-generated code, explicitly treating its qualitative interaction study as complementary to quantitative productivity research rather than as contrary evidence. It materially develops the proposition by distinguishing acceleration—executing an existing plan—from exploration—using Copilot to help formulate an approach—and by documenting the verification and debugging burden generated code can impose. It further proposes less intrusive generation and always-on validation as design responses. Internal variation matters: Copilot can preserve flow, provide useful starting points and support exploration, yet generated code may be harder to understand and debug; these observations come from a short, 20-participant qualitative study and do not estimate a comparative productivity effect or establish how broadly the findings generalise.

qs.q: Further, instead of skewing quantitative answers to predefined research questions, we chose the grounded theory approach, with the general goal of finding patters in programmers’ behavior when they interact with Copilot; we believe this approach is complementary to the quantitative studies.
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

qs.q: On the flip side, participants found it more difficult to spot an error in code generated by Copilot.
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

elens.an: The sources from this curated 2023–2024 period collectively accept the proposition that coding copilots can accelerate a narrowly defined task while leaving consequential human interaction and verification work outside that completion-time measure. They materially develop the proposition through complementary evidence: the randomized trial supplies causal evidence of a large reduction in time to the first commit passing the test suite among task completers, whereas CUPS decomposes the surrounding work into prompting, waiting, editing, deferred thought and verification, including checking performed after acceptance. The principal internal variation is methodological rather than directional. The trial has an unaided control but measures a bounded task and does not capture maintainability or downstream checking costs; CUPS provides granular behavioral evidence but has no no-Copilot baseline, so its observed interaction time cannot establish a net productivity penalty or contradict the trial’s speed gain. Experience-related patterns are also unsettled: subgroup results differ across benefit and acceptance measures and do not establish a general novice–expert effect. Broader claims about career access, long-term code quality or other professional domains remain prospective or unsupported by these studies.

elens.an: The sole supplied current-wave source cannot be positioned substantively for or against the proposition. Its fragment establishes an AI/control sample with 180 task-level observations and reports participants’ prior familiarity with coding assistants, but the interleaved numerical outcomes lack usable headings. It therefore provides no interpretable evidence about completion speed, verification workload, fatigue, code quality or net productivity. This evidentiary incompleteness is consistent with the proposition’s caution that checking costs must be distinguished from completion-time gains, but consistency with that caution is not affirmative support. With only this fragment, there is no meaningful source-level variation to compare; the material variation is instead between interpretable participant characteristics and uninterpretable outcome values.
